name: OMK 2A Psych Exam 2 — Batch 4: Substance Use, Toxidromes & Altered Mental Status

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department from the county jail 14 hours after intake because of severe abdominal cramping, six episodes of watery diarrhea, and vomiting. He is restless, repeatedly yawning, and asks for a blanket despite a room temperature of 22°C (72°F). Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg. Examination shows 7-mm pupils bilaterally, piloerection over both forearms, profuse lacrimation and rhinorrhea, and diffuse muscle aching without rigidity. There are healed linear scars over both antecubital fossae. He is fully oriented, speech is clear, and there are no hallucinations, tremor, or seizure activity. Fingerstick glucose is 96 mg/dL and noncontrast CT of the abdomen shows no acute abnormality. Which of the following best describes this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation: Opioid withdrawal is the head-to-toe mirror image of intoxication, described by patients as the worst flu they have ever had: piloerection and chills, lacrimation and rhinorrhea, yawning, gastrointestinal cramping with diarrhea and vomiting, muscle aches, tachycardia, and — the single most useful finding — mydriasis. Intoxication is dry and pinpoint; withdrawal is wet and wide. The 14-hour interval since incarceration cut off his supply, and the antecubital scars mark the route. Board pearl — opioid withdrawal is miserable but not life-threatening, which is exactly why alcohol and sedative-hypnotic withdrawal are managed far more aggressively; the fear of going through it again, not the danger of it, is what drives return to use.  [Learning objectives: LO 010, 026]

wrongExplanations.0: Alcohol withdrawal at this interval would be expected to produce tremor, and progression carries hallucinosis and seizures at 24 to 48 hours. He has no tremor, no hallucinations, and no seizure activity — and alcohol withdrawal does not produce lacrimation, rhinorrhea, and piloerection.
wrongExplanations.1: Cocaine intoxication causes mydriasis and sympathetic activation, but it produces euphoria, paranoia, and tactile hallucinations rather than diarrhea, vomiting, lacrimation, and rhinorrhea, and it would not be precipitated simply by 14 hours in custody.
wrongExplanations.3: Opioid intoxication is the opposite picture: euphoria, CNS depression, decreased gag reflex, and pinpoint pupils, progressing to respiratory depression. His pupils are 7 mm and he is fully alert with a respiratory rate of 20/min.
wrongExplanations.4: Phencyclidine intoxication produces belligerence, psychomotor agitation, analgesia, and both horizontal and vertical nystagmus. He is cooperative, oriented, and has no nystagmus described.
wrongExplanations.5: Sedative-hypnotic intoxication produces ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, and CNS depression. His speech is clear, he is fully oriented, and he is hyperadrenergic rather than depressed.

questions.eli5: He got locked up and could not get his usual drug, so his body went into the opposite state. Runny nose, watery eyes, goosebumps, diarrhea, and big wide pupils are the flu-like picture of opioid withdrawal.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive in a restroom. Respirations are 6/min and shallow, pulse is 58/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Examination shows 2-mm pupils bilaterally and an absent gag reflex. She is given naloxone 0.4 mg IV; within 2 minutes her respirations increase to 14/min, she opens her eyes, and she answers questions appropriately. Forty minutes later the nurse reports that she has become difficult to rouse. Repeat examination shows respirations of 7/min, oxygen saturation of 88% on room air, and 2-mm pupils. Fingerstick glucose is 104 mg/dL and noncontrast CT of the head shows no acute abnormality. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: B. Administer a repeat dose of naloxone
E. Administer activated charcoal via nasogastric tube
questions.explanation: Naloxone is a competitive mu-opioid antagonist with a half-life shorter than that of most opioids, so re-sedation as it wears off is expected rather than surprising — the patient must be redosed or observed, and this is the single most important practical fact about the drug. Her recurrent pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression confirm the opioid is still on board. Board pearl — naloxone is dosed to restore respiratory drive, not to wake the patient fully or to punish them; overshooting precipitates acute withdrawal, and its other adverse effects are arrhythmia with rapid IV push and rare flash pulmonary edema from the catecholamine surge.  [Learning objectives: LO 013, 091]

wrongExplanations.0: Flumazenil is the benzodiazepine-site antagonist and would do nothing for opioid-mediated respiratory depression. It also risks precipitating withdrawal seizures in a benzodiazepine-dependent patient, and her pinpoint pupils point to an opioid rather than a sedative-hypnotic.
wrongExplanations.2: Naltrexone is a long-acting oral antagonist for maintenance treatment after detoxification, not an acute reversal agent. Giving it to a patient with opioid still on board would precipitate prolonged, unmanageable withdrawal.
wrongExplanations.3: Buprenorphine induction is a maintenance strategy that requires the patient to already be in withdrawal, and starting a partial agonist in an obtunded, hypoxic patient does not address the immediate respiratory emergency.
wrongExplanations.4: Activated charcoal requires a protected airway and intact mental status; giving it to a patient with a respiratory rate of 7/min and an absent gag reflex risks aspiration, and it does nothing about the opioid already absorbed.

questions.eli5: The reversal medicine wore off faster than the drug it was reversing, so she started slipping back under. The fix is simply to give another dose and keep watching her.

questions.stem: Withdrawal from which of the following substances carries the highest risk of death?
questions.explanation: Alcohol withdrawal is the most dangerous withdrawal syndrome, killing through seizures and delirium tremens, which is precisely why alcohol detoxification is managed far more aggressively than opioid or stimulant withdrawal. The timeline to hold onto is minor symptoms first, then alcoholic hallucinosis and withdrawal seizures at roughly 24 to 48 hours, then delirium tremens peaking around day 2 and potentially lasting up to a week. Board pearl — sedative-hypnotic withdrawal is dangerous for the same reason, and barbiturate withdrawal is worse still, adding life-threatening cardiovascular collapse and requiring inpatient monitored detoxification.  [Learning objectives: LO 010, 091]

wrongExplanations.1: Cannabis withdrawal is mild, producing irritability, sleep disturbance, and decreased appetite. It is increasingly recognized as real, but it is not dangerous.
wrongExplanations.2: Cocaine withdrawal produces hypersomnolence, bradycardia, malaise, depression, and intense craving. It carries suicide risk from the depressive crash but not direct physiologic lethality.
wrongExplanations.3: Nicotine withdrawal causes irritability, poor concentration, and craving. It is a major barrier to cessation but is not physiologically dangerous.
wrongExplanations.4: Opioid withdrawal is intensely uncomfortable — the worst flu ever — with cramping, diarrhea, mydriasis, and autonomic surge, but it is explicitly not life-threatening in the way depressant withdrawal is.

questions.eli5: Coming off alcohol is the one that can actually kill you, through seizures and a dangerous confusion called delirium tremens. That is why alcohol detox gets treated so much more carefully than the others.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department unresponsive, with an empty prescription bottle of phenobarbital found beside him. Temperature is 35.1°C (95.2°F), pulse is 48/min, respirations are 6/min, and blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg. Examination shows sluggish pupillary responses, horizontal nystagmus, diminished bowel sounds, and generalized hypotonia; there is no rigidity and no clonus. Naloxone 0.4 mg IV produces no change, and flumazenil 0.2 mg IV likewise produces no change. Fingerstick glucose is 88 mg/dL and noncontrast CT of the head shows no acute abnormality. He is intubated for airway protection and given intravenous fluids. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional step in management?
choices: C. Administer a higher repeat dose of flumazenil
D. Administer sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine
questions.explanation: There is no antidote for barbiturate poisoning. Barbiturates are weak acids, so alkalinizing the urine with sodium bicarbonate ion-traps the ionized drug in the renal tubule and prevents reabsorption, enhancing elimination — that plus aggressive supportive care is the treatment. The lack of response to both naloxone and flumazenil is the buried clue that neither an opioid nor a benzodiazepine is responsible. Board pearl — the benzodiazepine versus barbiturate contrast is high-yield: benzodiazepines increase the frequency of chloride channel opening and have a real ceiling effect and an antidote, whereas barbiturates increase the duration of opening, have no ceiling, and have no antidote, which is what makes them far more lethal in overdose.  [Learning objectives: LO 010, 013, 026]

wrongExplanations.0: Cyproheptadine is the 5-HT2 antagonist used for serotonin syndrome, which requires clonus, hyperreflexia, and hyperthermia after a serotonergic agent. He is hypothermic, hypotonic, and areflexic in presentation, with no serotonergic exposure.
wrongExplanations.1: Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity, which presents with hyperthermia, dry flushed skin, mydriasis, and delirium. He is hypothermic and obtunded, not agitated and dry, and a cholinesterase inhibitor would worsen his bradycardia of 48/min.
wrongExplanations.2: Flumazenil already failed, which is diagnostic information rather than a dosing problem: it antagonizes the benzodiazepine site, and barbiturates bind a different site on the GABA-A receptor. Escalating it adds seizure risk without benefit.
wrongExplanations.4: Dantrolene blocks sarcoplasmic calcium release to treat the muscle rigidity of neuroleptic malignant syndrome and malignant hyperthermia. He is hypotonic and hypothermic, so there is no rigidity-driven hyperthermia to treat.

questions.eli5: This drug has no antidote — the two reversal medicines they tried did nothing. Making his urine more alkaline traps the drug in the urine so his kidneys can flush it out instead of reabsorbing it.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with alcohol use disorder who has been abstinent for 6 weeks comes to the emergency department 25 minutes after developing intense facial flushing, a throbbing headache, nausea with three episodes of vomiting, and weakness. He states that he used a friend's alcohol-based mouthwash before a job interview. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg, dropping to 82/50 mm Hg on standing. Examination shows flushed skin over the face and upper chest and no rigidity, clonus, or nystagmus. He takes one medication prescribed at his last addiction-medicine visit. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and electrocardiogram are unremarkable. Which of the following medications is he most likely taking?
questions.explanation: Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, blocking the conversion of acetaldehyde to acetate. Any alcohol exposure — including hidden sources such as mouthwash, cooking wine, or some cold preparations — lets acetaldehyde accumulate and produces an intense, deliberately aversive reaction: flushing, headache, nausea and vomiting, weakness, orthostatic hypotension, and respiratory difficulty. This is negative reinforcement by design and requires informed patient buy-in, since the reaction itself can warrant an emergency visit. Board pearl — the one-step enzymatic block is the entire mechanism and is worth being able to draw; rare adverse effects of the drug itself are hepatitis, optic neuritis, and peripheral neuropathy.  [Learning objectives: LO 001, 005, 006, 015]

wrongExplanations.0: Acamprosate is an NMDA antagonist and GABA-A agonist that supports abstinence by mirroring alcohol's own mechanism. It causes no aversive reaction on alcohol exposure; its practical drawback is three-times-daily dosing that hurts adherence.
wrongExplanations.1: Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist used off-label in alcohol use disorder. It produces sedation and muscle relaxation, not an acetaldehyde flush reaction.
wrongExplanations.3: Gabapentin is another recognized off-label option for alcohol use disorder, causing sedation and dizziness. It has no interaction with alcohol that produces flushing and vomiting.
wrongExplanations.4: Naltrexone is a mu-opioid antagonist used for craving management and can be started while a patient is still drinking, precisely because it produces no aversive reaction to alcohol.

questions.eli5: His medicine blocks the enzyme that clears the toxic breakdown product of alcohol. Even the alcohol in mouthwash was enough to make that product pile up and give him an instant, awful hangover — which is exactly what the drug is designed to do.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer completed a 5-day inpatient alcohol detoxification 2 weeks ago and has remained abstinent since. He wishes to start medication to help maintain abstinence. His pain is controlled with extended-release oxycodone 40 mg PO twice daily, which his oncologist intends to continue indefinitely. He states he is not prepared to commit to a regimen in which any alcohol exposure would make him acutely ill. Aspartate aminotransferase is 28 U/L, alanine aminotransferase is 31 U/L, total bilirubin is 0.8 mg/dL, and serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Vital signs are within normal limits and he has no asterixis or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: Two constraints decide this. He requires ongoing opioid analgesia, which rules out any opioid antagonist, and he has explicitly declined aversive therapy. Acamprosate is an NMDA-receptor antagonist and GABA-A agonist used for relapse prevention after detoxification is complete — exactly where he is — and it is renally cleared and liver-safe, which matters in oncology patients. Board pearl — the practical limitation to counsel him about is three-times-daily dosing, which is the main reason adherence suffers; naltrexone can be started while a patient is still drinking, whereas acamprosate is a post-detox maintenance agent.  [Learning objectives: LO 001, 005, 006, 015]

wrongExplanations.1: Disulfiram is aversive by design and requires informed patient buy-in, which he has explicitly withheld. Prescribing it to a patient who has said he does not want that arrangement is both ineffective and unsafe.
wrongExplanations.2: Naltrexone is a mu-opioid antagonist and is specifically avoided in patients taking opioids for pain — it would block his oxycodone and precipitate acute withdrawal along with uncontrolled cancer pain.
wrongExplanations.3: Nalmefene is also an opioid antagonist, so it fails for exactly the same reason as naltrexone, and it is an off-label agent rather than a primary choice.
wrongExplanations.4: Topiramate is a recognized off-label option that students should be able to identify, but it is not a primary agent for alcohol use disorder when a first-line drug is available and appropriate.

questions.eli5: Two of these medicines block the same receptor his cancer pain medicine needs, so they are off the table. He also does not want the one that makes you violently sick if you drink. That leaves acamprosate, which is safe with his liver and his pain treatment.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his girlfriend because of chest pain and agitation that began 1 hour ago. He is picking repeatedly at his forearms and states that he can feel insects moving beneath his skin, though no lesions other than excoriations are visible. He is convinced that people in the waiting room have been sent to watch him. Temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F), pulse is 122/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 178/104 mm Hg. Examination shows 8-mm pupils, diaphoresis, perforation of the nasal septum, and marked erosion of the maxillary gingiva. Electrocardiography shows sinus tachycardia with 1-mm ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads. Which of the following best describes this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation: Cocaine blocks reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin — the dopamine transporter most potently — and additionally blocks sodium channels. That combination produces impaired judgment, mydriasis, paranoid ideation, tactile hallucinations classically described as bugs crawling under the skin, and genuine cardiac danger including angina and sudden cardiac death. The buried clues that separate it from the very similar stimulant next to it are anatomic: nasal septal perforation from insufflation and gingival erosion from application to the gums. Board pearl — the sodium-channel blockade is why cocaine chest pain is a true cardiac emergency rather than an anxiety symptom.  [Learning objectives: LO 010, 026]

wrongExplanations.0: Alcohol withdrawal produces tremor, anxiety, autonomic hyperactivity, and in severe cases seizures and delirium tremens. It does not produce mydriasis with tactile hallucinations, and there is no nasal or gingival finding to explain.
wrongExplanations.1: Amphetamine intoxication is the closest competitor and shares euphoria, grandiosity, mydriasis, hypertension, tachycardia, and paranoia. What it does not explain are the tactile hallucinations specifically attributed to cocaine and the route-specific findings of septal perforation and gingival erosion.
wrongExplanations.2: LSD is a serotonin agonist producing visual illusions and perceptual distortion with generally preserved insight. It is not addictive, is managed by talking the patient down, and does not cause coronary vasospasm or septal perforation.
wrongExplanations.3: Phencyclidine intoxication produces belligerence, impulsivity, profound analgesia, and the signature combination of horizontal and vertical nystagmus. None of these is described here.
wrongExplanations.5: Opioid withdrawal produces mydriasis but with lacrimation, rhinorrhea, piloerection, and diarrhea rather than hypertension with chest pain and tactile hallucinations.

questions.eli5: He feels bugs crawling under his skin, is paranoid, and has chest pain — and his nose and gums are eaten away from how the drug was taken. That whole package points to cocaine, which also blocks channels in the heart and can cause a real heart attack.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man comes to the office 3 days after abruptly stopping a 5-day methamphetamine binge. He reports sleeping 14 to 16 hours daily, eating far more than usual, and feeling that nothing is enjoyable; he describes a pervasive sense that his life has no purpose. He denies hallucinations, paranoia, and suicidal ideation. He has no prior psychiatric history and no history of depressed mood outside periods of drug use. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 62/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Examination shows 3-mm reactive pupils, no diaphoresis, no piloerection or lacrimation, no tremor, and normal bowel sounds. Which of the following best describes this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation: Withdrawal from a stimulant is the mirror image of its intoxication. Where amphetamine intoxication brings euphoria, grandiosity, mydriasis, prolonged wakefulness, anorexia, hypertension, and tachycardia, withdrawal brings anhedonia, hypersomnolence, increased appetite, and the distinctive existential crisis this patient describes. His vital signs and pupils are normal, which fits a syndrome without autonomic instability. Board pearl — the organizing rule is that uppers cause psychosis during intoxication while downers cause psychosis during withdrawal, so amphetamine withdrawal specifically does not produce psychosis, and its absence here supports the diagnosis rather than arguing against it.  [Learning objectives: LO 010, 026]

wrongExplanations.0: Alcohol withdrawal produces tremor, anxiety, insomnia, and autonomic hyperactivity progressing to seizures and delirium tremens. He is sleeping excessively, has no tremor, and is hemodynamically normal.
wrongExplanations.2: Cocaine intoxication produces mydriasis, hypertension, tachycardia, paranoia, and tactile hallucinations. He has 3-mm pupils, normal vital signs, and no psychotic symptoms — and he stopped using 3 days ago.
wrongExplanations.3: A major depressive episode requires 5 or more symptoms including depressed mood or anhedonia for at least 2 weeks. He is 3 days out and has never had depressed mood outside periods of drug use, so the duration and the explicit absence of an independent mood history both fail.
wrongExplanations.4: Opioid withdrawal produces mydriasis, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, piloerection, cramping, and diarrhea. Each of those is explicitly absent on his examination, which is why those negatives are stated.

questions.eli5: Coming off a stimulant flips everything the drug was doing. Instead of wide awake and not hungry, he now sleeps all day, eats constantly, and feels like nothing matters.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after he punched through a storefront window. He is combative with staff, requires four-point restraint, and shouts that the officers are 'not real people.' He does not react when a 4-cm laceration on his forearm with visible extensor tendon is probed, and he attempts to stand on a leg that radiographs later show to be fractured. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 168/98 mm Hg. Examination shows 5-mm pupils and nystagmus that is present on both horizontal and vertical gaze. There is no lacrimation, rhinorrhea, piloerection, or diarrhea, and no nasal septal abnormality. Fingerstick glucose is 102 mg/dL. Which of the following best describes this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation: Phencyclidine is an NMDA antagonist, and its intoxication picture is belligerence, impulsivity, psychomotor agitation, homicidality, psychosis, and delirium. The finding that clinches it is nystagmus present on both horizontal AND vertical gaze — vertical nystagmus in particular is the signature. The clinically dangerous feature is profound analgesia: he probes a tendon-deep laceration without reacting and tries to weight-bear on a fractured leg, so patients sustain severe unnoticed injuries and require a careful trauma survey. Board pearl — PCP withdrawal is its own entity, marked by fever, tachycardia, and seizures.  [Learning objectives: LO 010, 026]

wrongExplanations.0: Alcohol intoxication produces emotional lability, slurred speech, ataxia, blackouts, and at high levels coma. It does not produce marked analgesia, hypertension with tachycardia, or vertical nystagmus.
wrongExplanations.1: Amphetamine intoxication causes euphoria, grandiosity, mydriasis, hypertension, tachycardia, and paranoia, but it does not produce analgesia deep enough to mask a fracture, and it does not cause vertical nystagmus.
wrongExplanations.2: Cocaine intoxication produces mydriasis, paranoia, tactile hallucinations, and cardiac risk. The examination explicitly notes no nasal septal abnormality, and cocaine does not cause vertical nystagmus or profound analgesia.
wrongExplanations.3: LSD is a serotonin agonist producing perceptual distortions with largely preserved insight and is managed by talking the patient down. It does not cause combativeness of this degree, analgesia, or vertical nystagmus.
wrongExplanations.4: Opioid withdrawal would produce lacrimation, rhinorrhea, piloerection, and diarrhea — all four explicitly absent — along with mydriasis rather than this agitated, analgesic, hypertensive picture.

questions.eli5: He is violent, thinks people are not real, and cannot feel a deep cut or a broken leg. Eyes that jerk both side to side and up and down are the giveaway for PCP.

questions.stem: Psychotic symptoms are most likely to occur in which of the following circumstances?
questions.explanation: The organizing rule is that uppers produce psychosis during intoxication and downers produce psychosis during withdrawal. Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant, and its withdrawal can produce alcoholic hallucinosis at 24 to 48 hours and delirium tremens peaking around day 2 — the classic depressant-withdrawal psychosis. The same logic applies to benzodiazepine and barbiturate withdrawal. Board pearl — apply this rule in both directions on an examination: amphetamine and cocaine intoxication cause psychosis while their withdrawal does not, and alcohol, benzodiazepine, and opioid intoxication generally do not cause psychosis while depressant withdrawal does.  [Learning objectives: LO 010, 032]

wrongExplanations.0: Amphetamine is an upper, so psychosis belongs to its intoxication phase. Its withdrawal produces anhedonia, hypersomnolence, increased appetite, and an existential crisis — explicitly without psychosis.
wrongExplanations.1: Cannabis withdrawal is mild, producing irritability, sleep disturbance, and reduced appetite rather than psychosis.
wrongExplanations.2: Nicotine withdrawal causes irritability, poor concentration, and craving. It has no psychotic component.
wrongExplanations.4: Opioid intoxication produces euphoria, CNS depression, decreased gag reflex, and pinpoint pupils, progressing to respiratory depression. As a downer, its psychosis risk sits in withdrawal, not intoxication — and even then it is far less prominent than with alcohol.

questions.eli5: Drugs that speed you up make you see things while you are on them. Drugs that slow you down make you see things when you stop. Alcohol slows you down, so the danger comes on the way off it.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with opioid use disorder is admitted for management of withdrawal after his supply was interrupted 16 hours ago. He has cramping, diarrhea, rhinorrhea, and marked anxiety, and his pulse is 116/min with a blood pressure of 158/96 mm Hg. He has been counseled at length about medications for opioid use disorder and states clearly and repeatedly that he does not want to be started on any opioid agonist or partial agonist, but he does want help with how he feels right now. He is fully alert, oriented, and has intact capacity. He has no seizure history and no concurrent alcohol or benzodiazepine use, and his urine toxicology screen is positive only for opiates. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for his current symptoms?
questions.explanation: Clonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that inhibits noradrenergic outflow and blunts the sympathetic surge common to nearly every withdrawal syndrome, partially blocking opioid withdrawal symptoms and easing the tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, and anxiety. It is the right answer here specifically because the patient has capacity and has declined agonist therapy, which removes the agents that would otherwise be preferred. Board pearl — clonidine is symptomatic support, not monotherapy for detoxification: it does not prevent withdrawal seizures, so it is explicitly not adequate alone for depressant withdrawal from alcohol, benzodiazepines, or barbiturates.  [Learning objectives: LO 015, 091]

wrongExplanations.1: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial mu agonist and an excellent treatment for opioid withdrawal and maintenance, but he has clearly and repeatedly declined partial agonist therapy and has the capacity to do so.
wrongExplanations.2: Methadone is a full mu agonist and likewise an effective option he has explicitly refused. It additionally carries QT prolongation risk and, for maintenance, requires enrollment in a licensed opioid treatment program.
wrongExplanations.3: Naloxone is a short-acting antagonist used to reverse opioid poisoning. Giving it to a patient already 16 hours into withdrawal would deepen his symptoms dramatically.
wrongExplanations.4: Naltrexone is a long-acting antagonist that requires completed detoxification before initiation — unlike its use in alcohol use disorder, where it can be started while the patient is still drinking. Given now, it would precipitate severe withdrawal.

questions.eli5: He does not want the opioid-based treatments, and that is his call. Clonidine calms the racing heart, sweating, and jitteriness that come from the body's alarm system going off during withdrawal.

questions.stem: Buprenorphine is co-formulated with naloxone in a 4:1 ratio for the treatment of opioid use disorder. Which of the following best explains how this combination deters misuse of the product?
choices: A. Naloxone abolishes buprenorphine's ceiling effect when the tablet is taken sublingually as directed
B. Naloxone accumulates with repeated sublingual dosing until it eventually blocks the mu receptor
C. Naloxone is poorly bioavailable by the sublingual route but precipitates withdrawal if the tablet is dissolved and injected
D. Naloxone prolongs the half-life of buprenorphine, which permits less frequent dosing and less diversion
E. Naloxone inhibits hepatic metabolism of buprenorphine, raising its plasma concentration and its street value
questions.explanation: The deterrent is route-based rather than pharmacodynamic. Naloxone has very poor oral and sublingual bioavailability, so when the combination product is taken as directed it is essentially inert and the patient receives only the buprenorphine effect. If the tablet or film is crushed, dissolved, and injected, the naloxone becomes bioavailable, competitively blocks the mu receptor, and precipitates acute withdrawal — making the misuse route punishing rather than rewarding. Board pearl — buprenorphine itself is a high-affinity partial agonist with a genuine ceiling effect, which is why it carries lower overdose risk than methadone, a full agonist.  [Learning objectives: LO 001, 005, 026]

wrongExplanations.0: Buprenorphine's ceiling effect comes from its own partial agonism at the mu receptor and is a safety feature, not something naloxone removes. Abolishing it would increase overdose risk, which is the opposite of the formulation's purpose.
wrongExplanations.1: Naloxone does not accumulate to therapeutic concentrations with sublingual dosing — the entire premise of the formulation is that essentially none of it is absorbed by that route.
wrongExplanations.3: Naloxone has no effect on buprenorphine's half-life. Buprenorphine's long duration of action comes from its high receptor affinity and slow dissociation.
wrongExplanations.4: Naloxone is a competitive receptor antagonist, not a metabolic inhibitor, and raising buprenorphine concentrations would increase rather than deter misuse potential.

questions.eli5: Taken the right way, under the tongue, the blocker part barely gets into the body and does nothing. If someone crushes it and injects it, the blocker suddenly works and throws them straight into withdrawal.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with opioid use disorder is seeking treatment after 4 years of daily intravenous fentanyl use; he last used 8 hours ago and is in early withdrawal. He wishes to begin a medication for opioid use disorder and is willing to consider either an agonist or a partial agonist. He has no history of alcohol use disorder. Aspartate aminotransferase is 32 U/L and alanine aminotransferase is 29 U/L. Serum potassium is 4.1 mEq/L and magnesium is 2.0 mg/dL. Electrocardiography shows normal sinus rhythm at 88/min with a QTc interval of 498 ms; a prior tracing from 2 years ago showed a QTc of 486 ms. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: Both agonist-based options would ordinarily be reasonable, so the ECG decides it. Methadone is a full mu agonist with well-documented QT prolongation, and this patient already has a QTc of 498 ms on two separate tracings with normal potassium and magnesium — meaning the prolongation is intrinsic and not a correctable electrolyte problem. Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist with a ceiling effect, lower overdose risk, and no comparable QT liability. Board pearl — buprenorphine's ceiling is what makes it the safer agonist-based choice generally, and the 4:1 co-formulation with naloxone adds a route-based misuse deterrent.  [Learning objectives: LO 001, 005, 006]

wrongExplanations.0: Clonidine blunts the autonomic symptoms of withdrawal but is symptomatic support only. It is not a medication for opioid use disorder and does nothing for the underlying disorder he is seeking to treat.
wrongExplanations.2: Methadone is an effective full agonist, but its QT prolongation risk makes it a poor choice at a QTc of 498 ms with normal potassium and magnesium. The stable prior value of 486 ms is the buried clue that this is his baseline rather than a transient derangement.
wrongExplanations.3: Naltrexone is an antagonist requiring completed detoxification before initiation. He last used 8 hours ago and is in early withdrawal, so starting it now would precipitate a severe reaction.
wrongExplanations.4: Naloxone is a short-acting antagonist for reversing acute opioid poisoning, not a maintenance treatment, and giving it to a patient already in withdrawal would worsen his symptoms.

questions.eli5: Two of these medicines could treat his addiction, but one of them stretches out the heart's electrical rhythm, and his is already stretched too far. Buprenorphine does the same job without that risk.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at an outdoor music festival where she had been dancing for several hours. Her friends report that she took a tablet obtained at the event and afterward drank 'a lot of water — she kept refilling her bottle.' In the emergency department she has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse is 134/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 138/86 mm Hg. Examination shows diaphoresis, 7-mm pupils, bruxism, and inducible ankle clonus. Fingerstick glucose is 92 mg/dL, and noncontrast CT of the head shows no acute abnormality. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is most likely to be found in this patient?
questions.explanation: MDMA reverses the serotonin transporter, flooding the synapse with serotonin — which explains the hyperthermia, diaphoresis, mydriasis, bruxism, and clonus. The distinct and separately testable complication is delayed hyponatremia, driven by the combination of heavy free-water intake and drug-related antidiuresis; the resulting cerebral edema is a classic cause of seizure in a festival setting. The buried clue is the repeated water refilling, which reads as sensible behavior and is actually the mechanism. Board pearl — the dramatic serotonergic findings tempt you toward a management answer, but the question asks what the laboratory will show, and free-water overload is what turns this from a toxidrome into a seizure.  [Learning objectives: LO 003, 026]

wrongExplanations.0: Hyperkalemia could follow rhabdomyolysis from prolonged exertion and hyperthermia, but it is a downstream, inconstant finding and does not explain a seizure the way acute hyponatremia does.
wrongExplanations.1: Hypercalcemia is unrelated to MDMA toxicity and would not be produced by exertion, hyperthermia, or free-water intake.
wrongExplanations.2: Hypoglycemia is an important cause of seizure in general, which is why a fingerstick is always checked — but hers is 92 mg/dL, a stated negative that closes this option.
wrongExplanations.3: Hypernatremia would result from free-water loss without replacement. She did the opposite, consuming large volumes of free water, which drives the sodium down rather than up.

questions.eli5: The drug she took floods the brain with a chemical that makes you hot and sweaty, and it also makes the body hold onto water. She drank huge amounts of water on top of that, her blood salt dropped, her brain swelled, and she had a seizure.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with bipolar I disorder is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of 4 days of progressive confusion and lethargy. He has taken valproate 1,500 mg PO daily for 3 years without a recent dose change, and takes no other medications. His wife reports no fever, no headache, no head trauma, and no alcohol or illicit drug use. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. Examination shows asterixis, no nuchal rigidity, no focal neurologic deficits, no rigidity, and no clonus. He has no jaundice, spider angiomata, or ascites. Serum studies show aspartate aminotransferase 34 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 29 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, sodium 139 mEq/L, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. Valproate concentration is 78 mcg/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
choices: A. Noncontrast CT of the head
questions.explanation: Valproate can cause a hyperammonemic delirium, and the critical teaching point is that it is not strictly dose-dependent — it can occur at any point in treatment and at a concentration squarely inside the therapeutic range, which is exactly the trap this stem sets with a level of 78 mcg/mL and normal aminotransferases. Any confused or altered patient on valproate should prompt an ammonia level regardless of how reassuring the dose and level look. The asterixis is the physical corroboration. Board pearl — this sits inside the broader rule-out ladder for altered mental status: exclude a substance or medication cause before attributing the picture to a medical or primary psychiatric process.  [Learning objectives: LO 032]

wrongExplanations.0: Head CT is reasonable in undifferentiated altered mental status, but he has no focal deficits, no head trauma, and no headache, and CT would not identify a metabolic encephalopathy — the asterixis points to a metabolic rather than structural cause.
wrongExplanations.1: EEG can confirm nonconvulsive status epilepticus, but nothing here suggests seizure activity, and an EEG would show only nonspecific slowing in a metabolic encephalopathy without naming the cause.
wrongExplanations.2: Lumbar puncture is indicated when meningitis or encephalitis is suspected. He is afebrile with no nuchal rigidity and no headache — three explicit negatives that close this option.
wrongExplanations.4: Repeating the level adds nothing: the concentration is already known to be therapeutic, and hyperammonemic delirium occurs independent of the level, which is precisely the fact being tested.
wrongExplanations.5: Urinary tract infection is the classic reversible cause of delirium in an elderly patient, but he is 44, afebrile, and has a specific drug exposure plus asterixis that point directly at a metabolic cause.

questions.eli5: His mood medicine can make ammonia build up in the blood and confuse him, even when the dose and blood level look perfectly normal. The hand flap on exam is the clue, so you check an ammonia level.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man with major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer disease is seen in a long-term care facility because of nightly restlessness, pacing the hallway, and shouting at staff between 8 PM and midnight. He has no hallucinations and no delusions, and he has not struck anyone or placed himself in physical danger. Over the past 3 weeks the facility has already implemented a consistent evening routine, reduced hallway noise and lighting changes, scheduled toileting, and daytime activity, without improvement. He has coronary artery disease and a prior myocardial infarction. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Urinalysis, complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and a medication review are unremarkable, and electrocardiography shows a QTc of 440 ms. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: Antipsychotics carry an FDA boxed warning for increased mortality when used for dementia-related psychosis in elderly patients — roughly a 1.6 to 1.7-fold increase over a 10-week window, about 4.5% versus 2.6%, with deaths largely cardiovascular or infectious. No antipsychotic is FDA-approved for this indication. Two constraints make that warning decisive here: he has coronary artery disease and a prior infarction, and he is not psychotic and not dangerous, so there is no symptom that justifies accepting the mortality risk. Trazodone is the recognized lower-risk off-label option for agitation and insomnia in dementia. Board pearl — counsel about its own risks of orthostatic hypotension, a genuine fall hazard in this population, and priapism.  [Learning objectives: LO 093]

wrongExplanations.0: Haloperidol carries the same boxed warning plus the highest extrapyramidal risk of the commonly used antipsychotics, and it prolongs the QT interval — a poor combination in an 82-year-old with established coronary disease and no psychotic symptoms.
wrongExplanations.1: Olanzapine carries the boxed warning and the heaviest metabolic burden, and it offers no advantage for a patient whose problem is evening restlessness rather than psychosis.
wrongExplanations.2: Quetiapine is often reached for in this population because of its role in Parkinson disease and Lewy body psychosis, but it still carries the boxed warning and adds marked orthostasis — and he has no psychosis to treat.
wrongExplanations.3: Risperidone is the atypical specifically named for dementia-related agitation in the elderly and would be the choice if an antipsychotic were genuinely warranted, but that threshold is not met here: he has no psychosis, no aggression toward others, and no danger to himself, and non-pharmacologic measures were tried for only one target.

questions.eli5: Antipsychotic medicines make older people with dementia more likely to die, and this man is not seeing things or hurting anyone — he is just restless at night. Trazodone is the safer choice for that, though it can make him dizzy when he stands.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with no psychiatric history is brought to the office by her husband because of 6 weeks of low mood, poor concentration, and early-morning awakening. She has hypertension, hypothyroidism, and chronic low back pain. Her husband reports that she has become forgetful and, twice this week, unusually irritable in a way he describes as unlike her. She takes several prescribed medications and two over-the-counter supplements, and her husband notes she has been taking 'more of the pain pills than the bottle says.' There is no reported secondary gain, no pending litigation or disability claim, and no evidence that she is exaggerating symptoms. According to the diagnostic sequence used in this course, which of the following should be established before a primary psychiatric disorder is diagnosed?
choices: A. That the symptoms are not attributable to intoxication, withdrawal, or a medication effect
B. That the symptoms are not better explained by an adjustment disorder
C. That the symptoms meet the full duration criteria for a major depressive episode
D. That the symptoms cause clinically significant functional impairment
E. That the symptoms do not fall into an other-specified or unspecified residual category
F. That a first-degree relative does not carry the same diagnosis
questions.explanation: The rule-out ladder runs in a fixed order: first exclude malingering and factitious production, then exclude a substance etiology including intoxication, withdrawal, and medication effects, then exclude an etiologic general medical condition, and only then diagnose a primary psychiatric disorder — after which you separate adjustment disorder from residual categories and from no disorder at all. The stem closes the first rung explicitly, with no secondary gain, no litigation, and no exaggeration, which places the substance and medication rung next. Her escalating analgesic use is the buried clue sitting on exactly that rung. Board pearl — a missed medical or drug cause treated as depression with one antidepressant after another is the classic avoidable failure mode this ladder exists to prevent.  [Learning objectives: LO 032]

wrongExplanations.1: Distinguishing adjustment disorder from a residual category is step 5 of the sequence, performed after a primary psychiatric disorder has already been considered — not before.
wrongExplanations.2: Duration criteria are applied when determining which specific primary diagnosis fits, at step 4. Applying them now would mean diagnosing a primary disorder before the substance and medical causes have been excluded.
wrongExplanations.3: Functional impairment is a criterion within most individual diagnoses rather than a gate that precedes the entire differential, and establishing it does nothing to exclude a drug or medical cause.
wrongExplanations.4: Separating other-specified and unspecified residual categories is step 5 in the sequence and comes after primary diagnosis, not before it.
wrongExplanations.5: Family history informs risk and can support a diagnosis, but the absence of an affected relative never excludes a psychiatric diagnosis and is not part of the rule-out sequence at all.

questions.eli5: Before you call something depression, you first make sure the person is not faking it, then make sure a drug or medicine is not causing it, then make sure a medical illness is not causing it. She has been taking extra pain pills, so that is the rung you are standing on.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after being found wandering in a town roughly 300 miles from his home. He carries no identification and cannot state his own name, date of birth, or where he lives. Investigation reveals that he disappeared 16 days ago and has been living in a rented room, working shifts at a restaurant under a different name, and that his coworkers describe him as consistently oriented, pleasant, and competent at his job. He has no history of head trauma. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows no focal deficits, and he recalls three of three objects at 5 minutes. Urine toxicology screening is negative, comprehensive metabolic panel is normal, and MRI of the brain shows no abnormality. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: B. Dissociative amnesia, with dissociative fugue
questions.explanation: Apparently purposeful travel away from home, coupled with amnesia for personal identity and adoption of a new name, defines dissociative fugue — which in DSM-5 is a specifier coded alongside dissociative amnesia rather than a stand-alone diagnosis. Everything else here exists to strip away competing explanations: no head trauma, normal neurologic examination, normal MRI, negative toxicology, and normal metabolic studies. Board pearl — most cases of dissociative amnesia and fugue resolve spontaneously without treatment, and the information is not permanently lost, only inaccessible.  [Learning objectives: LO 030]

wrongExplanations.0: Depersonalization/derealization disorder involves feeling detached from one's own body or surroundings while reality testing stays fully intact. There is no loss of identity or purposeful travel, and the patient knows the feelings are not literally true.
wrongExplanations.2: Dissociative identity disorder requires two or more distinct personality states plus recurrent gaps in recall, typically on a background of severe early childhood abuse. Living under one assumed name is not an alternate identity state, and his coworkers describe a single consistent presentation.
wrongExplanations.3: Factitious disorder requires conscious, intentional falsification of symptoms to occupy the sick role. He was working shifts and functioning competently, seeking no medical attention at all until police found him.
wrongExplanations.4: Malingering requires conscious feigning for an external incentive such as money, avoiding legal consequences, or obtaining drugs. No external gain is described, and 16 days of ordinary restaurant work is not a plausible route to secondary gain.
wrongExplanations.5: Transient global amnesia is an abrupt anterograde amnesia lasting under 24 hours in which personal identity is characteristically preserved. He is 16 days out, has lost identity specifically, and forms new memories normally — he recalls three of three objects at 5 minutes.

questions.eli5: He traveled far from home, forgot who he was, and started a whole new life under a different name for two weeks — but his brain scan and blood tests are normal and he was not pretending. Traveling plus forgetting your own identity is called a fugue.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman is admitted for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy and is kept nil per os beginning at midnight. At 6 PM the following day, roughly 18 hours after her last oral intake, she reports a throbbing bilateral headache, marked fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and irritability. She has no nausea, photophobia, or neck stiffness. On further history she reports drinking five cups of coffee daily for the past 6 years and denies alcohol, tobacco, opioid, and benzodiazepine use, which is corroborated by a negative urine toxicology screen. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 68/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. Examination shows no tremor, no diaphoresis, no piloerection, no lacrimation, and no mydriasis; neurologic examination is normal. Which of the following best explains her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Caffeine dependence can develop in as little as 1 week of regular use, and withdrawal begins 12 to 24 hours after the last dose and can last up to a week. The syndrome is headache and fatigue, often with poor concentration and irritability, and it is easy to miss in hospitalized patients whose usual intake stops abruptly with nil-per-os orders. Her 18-hour interval sits exactly in that window. Board pearl — this is a genuinely common inpatient confounder that gets misattributed to anxiety or to the underlying illness, and it is corrected by simply allowing caffeine once the patient can take oral intake.  [Learning objectives: LO 026, 099]

wrongExplanations.0: Alcohol withdrawal produces tremor, anxiety, insomnia, and autonomic hyperactivity progressing toward seizures and delirium tremens. She has no tremor, no diaphoresis, normal vital signs, and denies alcohol use with a corroborating toxicology screen.
wrongExplanations.1: Benzodiazepine withdrawal produces anxiety, insomnia, tremulousness, nausea and vomiting, transient hallucinations, and potentially seizures. None of these is present, and she denies benzodiazepine use with a negative screen.
wrongExplanations.3: Nicotine withdrawal is a genuine consideration in a hospitalized patient, but she denies tobacco use, and its predominant features are craving and irritability rather than a prominent throbbing headache.
wrongExplanations.4: Opioid withdrawal would produce mydriasis, lacrimation, piloerection, cramping, and diarrhea — each of those is explicitly documented as absent, which is why those negatives are listed.

questions.eli5: She drinks five coffees a day and the hospital stopped her from eating or drinking. About eighteen hours later her body noticed the missing caffeine and gave her a pounding headache and fatigue.

questions.stem: A man who has injected heroin daily for several years is enrolled in a research study. When he is shown a syringe and a tourniquet in a laboratory setting, without any drug being administered, monitoring shows a measurable fall in his heart rate and a drop in skin temperature — the same physiologic changes his body mounts to oppose the drug's effects when he actually uses. Which of the following types of tolerance does this best illustrate?
questions.explanation: Conditioned tolerance occurs when environmental cues previously paired with drug administration — the paraphernalia, the setting, the ritual — come to trigger the body's compensatory response on their own, before any drug is present. This is classical conditioning applied to physiology, and it has real clinical consequences: it explains why cues drive craving without any drug on board, and why using the same dose in an unfamiliar setting, where the conditioned compensatory response is not triggered, can produce a fatal overdose. Board pearl — the six types to keep straight are innate, acquired pharmacokinetic, acquired pharmacodynamic in its acute and chronic forms, behavioral, and conditioned.  [Learning objectives: LO 026]

wrongExplanations.0: Acquired pharmacodynamic tolerance is a change at the target itself — reduced receptor number or altered channel signaling acutely, and gene expression changes chronically. It requires the drug to be present to matter and does not explain a response to the sight of equipment.
wrongExplanations.1: Acquired pharmacokinetic tolerance is upregulation of metabolizing enzymes or transporters so that more drug is cleared. It affects drug concentration and cannot produce a physiologic change when no drug has been given.
wrongExplanations.2: Behavioral tolerance is a learned compensatory behavior — a person practicing walking a straight line while intoxicated so the impairment is less visible. It is a skill under voluntary control, not an autonomic response to a cue.
wrongExplanations.3: Innate tolerance is pre-existing genetic or pharmacokinetic variation present before any exposure. It would not be created by years of use and would not be cue-dependent.

questions.eli5: His body learned that needles and tourniquets mean the drug is coming, so it starts pushing back before he even uses. Just seeing the gear makes his heart slow down.
